en: Having bowed to the crown-jewel of matted locks, the illustrious Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa), and my teacher who possesses total attentiveness,
I shall proclaim the *Jaṭāmaṇi* together with the verses known as the *Śrījaṭāvalśas*. 1.
Having thoroughly examined all the treatises on the Śikṣā and other branches, for the easy understanding of those who know the characteristics of the meaning of the Vedas,
this Maṇi of Jaṭā is being manifested by the wise Nema-Bhairava through the grace and side-glance of Paraśiva.
May the Goddess of Speech, who always studies the Vedas and Śāstras, reside within the mouth of that person [who reads this].
I bow to that Veṅkaṭeśa, whose mother speaks what is untrue;
3. I bow to that Śaṅkara, the teacher of the world, with whom the daughter of that supreme Lord has attained a truly non-dual oneness that brings joy to the people here. 4.
One who knows the Prātiśākhya and other treatises, is proficient in all the Śikṣās,
and possesses a subtle and capable intellect, is fit to explain the *jaṭā* [arrangement].
Having set aside the *jaṭā*, one may speak of the *anuloma* and other forms which possess diverse meanings.
He indeed falls into hell, like one who destroys the proper accent and phonetic color [of Vedic recitation].
The authority for this is found in the first chapter of the *Prātiśākhya*, regarding the substitution of the letter *r* (*repha*), from the word "śabda" and from the archaic term "na dhāma."
In the *jaṭā* meter, there are five types of *saṃdhi* based on the distinction between *ārṣa* (Vedic) and *pauruṣa* (human).
That which is at the beginning and end is designated as *ārṣa*, while the other, being joined (*śliṣṭa*), is *pauruṣa*.
In the *trikrama* meters, there are eight types of *saṃdhi*, with two each at the beginning and the end.
Those very same junctions (*sandhi*) here are designated as *ārṣa* (of the seers), whereas these others are non-*ārṣa*.
Having recited two words in their regular order, then out of order, and then in reverse order, joined with their proper accents— that is considered the *jaṭā* [recitation].
That which arises from logic, from favor, or from an illustration is called *viloma*; when a *sandhi* occurs there according to logic, it is designated as *nyāyaprāpta*.
Where a *sandhi* that is not manifest in the Vedic (*ārṣa*) style should appear in the *jaṭā* [meter], [it is so].
Therefore, the example of the *sandhi* mentioned in the *Brāhmaṇa-āraṇyaka* is stated:

one should recite the first word once and the second word twice; then, having joined them according to the rules of *sandhi*, one should recite the first word once again—this is called *jaṭā* by the wise. 8–9.
The *jaṭā* of the *trikrama* should be known; having first stated the *krama*, it is then repeated as the middle, the beginning, and the end of the beginning, which is supreme.
Having ascended the three words together with their euphonic combinations (*sandhi*) in the *trikrama*.
Having descended according to the rule, the re-ascension is prescribed.
In the case of the three-step [movement], there is a descent of three steps;
likewise, their subsequent ascension is desired to be from the rear toward the front.
One should speak of two words, six words, and likewise nine words,
according to the specific distinctions of vowels and consonants, and sequentially in the three-fold progression (trikrama).
This concerns the non-differentiation of vowels and consonants within the pair of words.
"Jaṭā is said to consist of distinct [units] through sequential utterance alone.

This is the technical rule (paribhāṣā) regarding elision (lopa), non-elision (alopa), the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva), the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva), the substitution of *y* (yatva), augments (āgama), and so forth.
And the *saṃhitā* [is established] exactly as it occurs in the *Jaṭā*, for it is just like that. 15.

Regarding the fires (*agni*) which suffer distress elsewhere due to what was previously done, the mention of the cause "in *agni*" was made because of the absence of the elision of the semi-vowel (*yaṇ-lopa*). 16.
Since a single word is indeed employed with reference to one [specific] inclusion,
it should not be accepted elsewhere as intended by Jaṭā;
likewise, even in the case of *aśvājanī*, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, [the same principle follows].
The form [of the vowel] is obtained through the scriptural tradition; therefore, there is elision in the case of *vilomaka*.

Likewise, in the case of "brāhmaṇāya" following "īta" or "upeta," although there is phonetic combination (*akṣara-saṃhitā*) there as well, the diphthong *ai* cannot occur here because of the predominance of the preceding [vowel]. 18–19.

When the *chatva* (the substitution of a palatal) has occurred for the letter *ś*, and subsequently the phonetic similarity (*varṇa-śliṣṭa*) [is applied], the original *nakāra* follows; therefore, the established form is *śnathad vṛtram*.
For when the vowel *u* in the word *anu* has been changed to *v*, [the following applies].
The established conclusion is that there shall be no elision of the letter *a* in the *jaṭā* [compound];

for when the vowel *u* occurs in the word *anu* and the letter *v* has been substituted [for *va*], there shall indeed be elision in the *jaṭā*, according to the rules of *saṃhitā* in the interval. 21–22.

For all [words], shortness occurs in the preceding *pauruṣa*; at the beginning and end it is long, while in the middle it is in the subsequent *pauruṣa*. That which has the quality of *pragraha* in the *ārṣa* [text] shall likewise have it in the *anārṣa*.
Even if the characteristics previously described are present, it would not occur anywhere in a human being (if that were the case).
If the mention of "two-footed" [beings] is intended to include both the Pradhāna and the Efficient Cause (nimitta),
then in the case of a reversal of order, it should be understood as applying to all [of them], whereas in the case of the sequential order, it applies only to one part.
When two words constitute a single compound (nimitta), even if one is absent, the sequence should be understood as being like *saṃhitā*; likewise, the *jaṭā* should be understood by the wise.
Furthermore, there is the elision (*lopa*) of particles such as *ca*, and also the elision of *m* and *o* when followed by another [vowel].

When *stha* or *stanbhu* follows, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *s* of *udaḥ*; however, when a consonant follows *ut*, the elision of the *s* of that which is preceded by *ut* is desired. But in the former case, when *an* or *ava* precede and an indeclinable (*avyaya*) stands [as the following word], there is elision of the *v*. (27–28)
In the absence of elision (lopābhāve), when *kvip* follows *makāra* and *rājate* follows, it is indicated without distinction because those [specific cases] alone are well-known.
Even in their reverse order, it applies to those alone; for others, no such rule is recorded.
The *avagraha* (the marker 'm') is that which is not elided when one says "yassaṃsāmi";
it should be understood by the wise as occurring elsewhere as well. That elision which follows remains [as it is] in the same way when there is a single grasping (*ekayā grahaṇe*). 30–31.
The elision of *m* (in the word *iti*) does not depend on a specific cause;

if a *guṇa* were to arise from a combined vowel (*pṛkta*) rather than a single phoneme (*apṛkta*), then a long vowel would follow that [single phoneme], whereas in other cases, there would be an augment (*āgama*). 32.

Alternatively, when there is a doubling of a letter (*ūbhāva*), for that reason the elision of the preceding [vowel] occurs even in a *saṃhitā* context; however, in the case of the *yajamāna* and *adhvaryu*, it occurs even in a non-*saṃhitā* context.
If [the vowel] has been elided in the Vedic text (*ārṣa*), it is performed by the wise, but not otherwise.

That which has been stated regarding the instruction on the nature of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) and *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*), this [treatise] effects that apprehension; it performs this function everywhere, and not otherwise.
The sequence should be understood as being like *saṃhitā*, as well as the *jaṭā* and other such transformations.

In cases of modification, addition, or elision, [a rule] partakes of the *saṃhitā*-operation as appropriate. However, when there is a prohibition of the cause (*nimitta*), the injunction does not occur by force of that cause.
But when there is no distinction in the indicator (*iṅgin*) and it is not counted, the injunction does not partake of the prohibition.

Furthermore, the presence of the *satva* (unchanged vowel) is not desired after a *kṛt* suffix due to its predominance; however, in this case, because the word "again" (*punaḥ*) serves as the cause, the *satva* is desired after a *kṛt* suffix when the word "again" follows in reverse order [as a compound].
38. After a *kṛt* suffix, the *satva* is desired following the word "again" (*punaḥ*) in a reversed [compound] construction.
By the rule *nāddhvara-*, the occurrence of the avagraha is prohibited [in cases like *patnī*].
(39) Since the letter *e* is preceded by a vowel, it is also indicative of a long vowel; furthermore, because of the mention of *patnī*, [the form] *gnāspatiḥ* is seen there. (40)
In the word *udatha*, the long vowel is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the short vowel as well;
likewise, in *prapara*, the short vowel is an indicator of the long vowel.
[This applies] because there is a prohibition in *dhaṣavati* and because the *kṣatra* here extends in every direction.

In the case of *ceṅgya*, *pade*, *nityam*, *nāvi*, *sūtre*, and *kṛdhī*, as well as after *ka*, *kha*, *pa*, and *eṣan*, when preceded by a vowel, there is a pause (*avagraha*) in the *saṃyāti* [section]. Herein are also *devariṣaḥ*, *cāviḥ*, *niriddhaḥ*, and *śaśvata upasaḥ*. (42–43)

Where there might be the elision of *mah*, there *ṣatva* does not occur in the word *pauruṣa*; because of the prohibition [of *ṣatva*], and because of the observation of both *mahi* and *sapta*. Furthermore, that which is joined with the vowel *ṛ* and the letter *r* is indeed the wind (*vāyu*) in the word *niḥśabda*.
The status of being a goat would necessarily follow for the buffalo, since it was spoken of by him [the sage].

Furthermore, when a contradiction between what is explicitly stated and what is more extensive is remembered in some cases, that which is explicitly stated is stronger; thus, the word "āviḥ" is the proof. 45–46.

Even when *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) would otherwise apply according to rules not specifically commenced [for this purpose], they do not pronounce it even after *pārī*, *adhi*, or *pūrva*; indeed,
many do not pronounce that which is obtained by rule as if it were *saṃhitā*.
It is said that at the time of tying the topknot, students [commit] that [text] to their arms;
if it were [already] mastered by the aged, the Śikṣā and the Prātiśākhya would be in contradiction.
They say that the Śikṣā is weak, just as a doe is [weak] compared to a lioness. 48–49.
It is proclaimed that the *Prātiśākhya* is authoritative regarding the *prakṛti* (original form),
and the *Śikṣā* is indeed authoritative regarding all non-Vedic (*anārṣa*) sandhis.
Regarding the *jaṭā* which is about to be described, there are the *kampasandhi*, vowel accents (*svara*), and so forth.
It should be applied with discernment by a skillful twice-born man.

(51) Indeed, they do not dance, nor even when another sound is raised loudly; for the letter *na* is marked by the doubling of the sphere [the anusvāra], and the letter *ta* is above it, as well as the letter *va*. (52)
A wise person should apply the substitution of *ṇ* for a preceding *n*, first and then for the following *ṭ*, because [the rule] is not explicitly shown in the sūtras;
whatever is not seen in the sūtras may occur by the force of other sūtras. 53.
The opinion is that there is no fault in accepting [the doubling] of an unmentioned consonant provided it is not in conflict;
otherwise, there would be a lack of smoothness for the letter *la* when it follows the *ṭa*-group (*ṭavarga*).
If it were otherwise, it would be in conflict because of the pause (*virāma*) and the absence of doubling. 54–55.

In the case of *aut*, *van*, *dau*, *tpareramṛtyāram*, and *propāva* when preceded by another [word], there shall be a pause (*pada*) even in the *svapāṭha* (recitation for oneself), provided that [the preceding word] does not end in *su*; this is as in the example *ṣuṣu*. Furthermore, whatever [word] has both *y* and *r* in its Vedic (*ārṣa*) form, it likewise [behaves] in the *pauruṣa* (human recitation).
When a vowel follows, there is a prohibition [of doubling] in that same manner; otherwise, it would not occur.

(57) When the letters *ya* and *ra* are absent and a different [consonant] is seen to be the subject of the rule, then the substitution of *ṣa* and *ṇa*, and so forth, must be applied everywhere as in the regular (anuloma) order. (58)

Wherever there may be a *yatva* (the substitution of *ya*), there the *tatva* (the substitution of *ta*) should likewise occur; and where there is a prohibition regarding the *jaṭā*, there the *tatva* should likewise occur. However, in the case of the *ārṣa* [text], wherever there is a *grahaṇa* (separate mention), the *prakṛti* (original form) remains as a *saṃhitā*.
Since it is the word of the Seer (*ārṣa*), the original form (*prakṛti*) may occur even at the beginning and end of a *jaṭā*;
likewise, in the case of *mithunī*, *yatva* (the substitution of *ya*) is desired in the reverse order because of its absence in the *saṃhitā* and because it is seen in the eight *mithunya* formulas.

In the case of *stomāya jyotiḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur because it is preceded by an unseparated (*anavagraha*) word; such being the case, there is no application [of the rule], and thus no prohibition is required, nor is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) recorded. (62)

The substitution of *ṣ* occurs only for that which is subject to reversion (*pratiprasava*), and not otherwise. (63) Furthermore, in the case of *su-ūro-hau*, the elided *visarga* there regains its status as *o* when followed by *r*, by virtue of the power of its subsequent re-mention. (64)
"Make us well-clothed and grant us divine food; may we not suffer the fault in this sacrifice and in our matted locks, for the fires have been satisfied.
This speech was undesirable.
The maxim beginning with "the three-word [rule]" applies to cases of elision and non-elision;

therein, if that which stands in the middle is joined with another, the property of the preceding does not exist. The rule concerning three words and so forth can only occur in the context of elisions and non-elisions.
Those who know the Vedas understand that one should not apply *pragraha* at the beginning;

furthermore, that which will be explained regarding [the sandhi of] *e* and *o* when occurring across multiple words is called *jaṭā* by another term, and in that case, there is no lack of unity. 67–68.

Wisdom (prajñā), however, is first seen sequentially in the matted locks (jaṭā); likewise, subsequently, it appears in the three steps and so forth, performing the functions of removing impurities (alopalopa).
Its status as the third is traditionally recorded from the "three steps" onwards, due to its preeminence.

For in the verses of the Ṛgveda and in the prose passages of the Brāhmaṇas, a repetition of two or three words and so forth is sufficient; since [the rule] applies up to five words, or even more than that,
it should be understood by the wise that this occurs everywhere as previously described.
Having surrounded him, may he arise again with vigor;

and may the sevenfold heat of this one who bestows gifts be favorable to us. O Agni, you who possess cattle, shine forth upon us! May your splendor be wondrous and abundant, and may it overcome all adversaries.
Flow onward, O Agni, beyond the sun and the sky;
likewise, through sacrifice, grant us long life, vigor, and breath itself.
O Agni, by means of that which unites you with the sacrificial steed in this common dwelling, may we attain strength.
In the case of *kramyāt*, *adhvanaḥ*, *bhavati*, *agre*, *pāvakaḥ*, and *arpayati*, as well as in the case of *viṣaye*, *iṅgaraḥ*, *eva*, *api*, *agraḥ*, and so forth, [the final vowel] is elided.
[The forms] *dadhikrāḥ*, *arpaṇaḥ*, *rakṣāḥ*, *ca*, *maryaśrīḥ*, and *janeva* [are also treated accordingly].
These [mantras] of his—Hiraṇyagarbha, Sañcārin, Anūpa, Aśvājani, and Agnayaḥ—as well as the Adhvaryu [mantra], may indeed be repeated;
for the five-word [formula] should be exactly as stated. 76–77.
Likewise, in the words of the Brahmins, there may be "alaṃ dvistripadādi" and so forth;

if, in the phrase "syāt tāṃ avidvān," an anusvāra is inserted, it should be understood that even by means of what is not an archaic (anārṣa) form, the inclusion of the letter 'a' and others is intended. 78.
Regarding the phrase "dyaur aha," the reason why the *ṇatva* (nasalization) is observed here is that it does not occur when [the words] remain in different locations; furthermore,
there is the manifestation of the fires born from the horse and the watchful one.
This was also indicated by Ātreya through the force of the mention of "hearing" (śruti).
There are two kinds of word-composition (*padasaṃhitā*) regarding words, syllables, limbs, and phonemes; these five compositions are spoken of when various words are uttered. 80–81.

By reciting the *saṃhitā*, the *pada*, the *krama*, and the *jaṭā*, one who knows the characteristics [of these modes] attains the eternal abode of Brahman. Indeed, the fruit that is proclaimed by the wise for the mere recitation of the *saṃhitā*— [is obtained through this]. 82.
One should know that [the merit] is doubled for a single word (*pada*), fourfold for a sequence (*krama*),
a hundredfold for the sequence of syllables (*varṇakrama*), and a thousandfold for the *jaṭā* arrangement;
likewise in the *Gāruḍapurāṇa*.
The knowledge of the Vedas is proclaimed as the supreme among all knowledges;
therefore, the gain of both heaven and liberation belongs only to one who gives that [knowledge], and not to one who does not.
Furthermore, the knowledge of Brahman is proclaimed as the highest among all knowledges.
Therefore, O King, from the gift of that [Veda], one obtains the fruit of all gifts.
In the Devīpurāṇa, it is said:
"For the twice-born, the Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good."
Then, through the practice of meditation upon that, he attains the Supreme Brahman.
(87) The wise man should cultivate that very [Brahman] and cause it to be imparted to his disciples;
through both its cultivation and its imparting, he attains the Supreme Brahman. (88)
The twice-born who, having studied the Vedas, exerts his efforts elsewhere,
quickly falls to the status of a Śūdra in this very life, along with his lineage.
For one devoid of Vedic knowledge, a web of other learning is useless.
Just as ornaments are useless for a woman who lacks a necklace around her neck,
so too is the study of the scriptures meaningless for those untrained in the Vedas.
What purpose is there in Vājapeya and other such sacrifices for one who has not been initiated?
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"The sonless obtains a son; the poor obtains wealth; one endowed with learning and study merges into the supreme Brahman. (92)
The nature of the Yajurveda is now described:
the Yajurveda has tawny eyes, a waist of kuśa grass, a broad neck, and a large skull; his feet are black and copper-colored, and he is born of the Kāśyapa lineage. (93)
In the Saṃbhava Parvan,
they recited repeatedly with clear tones and Yajus mantras that illuminate the meanings, by those who were experts in the distinctions between the matted locks and the syllables. 94

In the Anuśāsana Parva, in the hymn to Nārada, and throughout the entire Saṃhitā, he was a master of the two-word sequence whether standing or occurring, as well as of the *jaṭā* (interwoven) arrangement. 95.
He who knows only the matted locks and understands the junctions of the Vedas is called Viṣṇu;
he who knows all junctions is proclaimed by the sages as Īśvara.
Those who are devoid of the sequence of the matted locks and the phonemes are merely day-dwellers (ignorant), even if they claim to know the Vedas.
They go to a terrible hell for as long as fourteen Indras [reign], until the root of the Jaṭāmaṇi is fully perfected. 97.
